passages.title: Man's creation, the way shown, the chains prepared
passages.tafsir:
These four ayat move from a human being who was **not a thing worth mentioning**, to his making from a mixed drop, to the giving of hearing and sight, to the road being shown him — and then to what has been prepared for those who disbelieve: chains, iron collars, and a blaze.

## The surah and its names

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that this surah, **Sūrah ad-Dahr**, has also been called **Sūrah al-Insān** ("Man") and **Sūrah al-Abrār** ("The Righteous"), citing *Rūḥ*. It describes, in that commentary's words, "the inception and end of human creation, reward and punishment of deeds, and the conditions of the Hereafter, Paradise and Hell" — and does so in a very effective, eloquent and elegant style.

Ibn Kathīr opens by recalling something recorded in **Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim** from Ibn ʿAbbās: that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to recite in the Morning prayer on Friday *Alif Lām Mīm — Tanzīl* (32:1–2) and *Hal atā ʿalā al-insān* (this surah).

## Ayah 1: a question that answers itself

**"Has there not been over man a period of time, when he was not a thing worth mentioning?"**

The ayah opens with **hal** — the Arabic particle that introduces a question. But Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points out that an interrogative construction is often used to emphasise a self-evident truth: put such a question to anyone at any time and the same answer comes back, with no other possibility. Ask a man in the middle of the day, "Is it not a day?" — the sentence is a question, yet the answer is predictable, and the asking only underlines how obvious it is. This is why some scholars say **hal** is used here in the sense of **qad**, "indeed". Either way, the meaning of the ayah is settled: there has come upon man a period of time in which he was nothing worth mentioning.

**"a period of time" — ḥīn min ad-dahr.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that the word *ḥīn* carries **nunation** (*tanwīn*) — the "n" sound at the end of an Arabic noun that marks it as indefinite — and that this indefiniteness signifies a long, unspecified period of time.

There is a fine point buried in the phrasing. Time *came upon* him. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the conclusion: this indicates that man did exist at that time in one form or another, though not in a way worth mentioning — because time could not have come upon him had he been in a state of **al-ʿadam al-maḥḍ**, pure non-existence. Hence the ayah does not say he was *nothing*, but that he was **not a thing worth mentioning**.

**Which period?** Two readings are given:

- **The womb.** Most commentators, says Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, take the "period of time" as the span from conception in the mother's womb until birth, normally nine months. That period covers all the stages of his creation — from a sperm-drop, to a body with organs, and then his acquiring life and soul. During this time neither his gender is known to anyone, nor his name, nor his shape or size. He is, in the commentary's word, **unmentionable**.
- **The wider reading.** The statement may also be taken in a wider sense: human creation begins with the drop that is produced by food, and that food, its source and its substance, existed in one form or another before. If that period is calculated, says Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, this long indefinite period of time can stretch into **thousands of years**.

Ibn Kathīr states the point plainly: Allah informs us that **He brought man into existence after he was not even a thing worth mentioning**, due to his lowliness and weakness.

**Why this is placed before us.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says that in this ayah Allah has drawn man's attention to a particular fact: if he uses his sense, he will discover his own reality, and he will have no choice but to have complete faith and unshaken belief in Allah, His Omniscience and His Omnipotence.

Then it offers a thought experiment. Suppose a person of seventy years reflects that about seventy-one years ago he was unmentionable in any way — even his parents had not imagined his particular existence, though they might have had a general concept of a child. What then caused his creation? What bewildering power drew together particles from different parts of the world to form a perfect human being, and made him an intelligent, hearing and seeing creature? Such a reflection, the commentary says, will spontaneously force such a person to confirm the Persian poet who says:

> Neither we were there, nor was there any demand from us. It is only Your mercy that listened to what we never said.

You were not there to ask. There was no demand from you. What answered was mercy.

## Ayah 2: the mixed drop, the test, and the two faculties

**"Verily, We have created man from Nuṭfah Amshāj, in order to try him, so, We made him hearer and seer."**

Ayah 1 posed the question; ayah 2, in Ibn Kathīr's reading, is Allah **explaining** it.

**Amshāj — "mixed".** Ibn Kathīr explains that the words *Mashaj* and *Mashij* mean something that is mixed together. Ibn ʿAbbās said of the phrase: "This means the fluid of the man and the fluid of the woman when they meet and mix." ʿIkrimah, Mujāhid, al-Ḥasan and ar-Rabīʿ ibn Anas all made statements similar to this. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that *amshāj* is the plural of *mashj*, meaning "a mixture", and that here it obviously refers to the male and female gametes, according to most commentators.

A second view is preserved: as cited in *Rūḥ ul-Maʿānī*, some commentators say *amshāj* refers to the four fluids of the body (blood, phlegm, choler and melancholy) of which the sperm is composed. This is the view of some, not of the majority — but Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws something valuable from it, and closes the discussion with **"And Allah knows best!"**

**Why the second view matters: an answer to the deniers of Resurrection.** Reflect carefully, says Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, and the cardinal fluids are made up of various kinds of nutriment; reflect further on man's food, and it contains elements of water and air from distant parts of the globe. Analyse man's present body and you will discover it is composed of elements and particles that were scattered "in every nook and corner of the world," which a marvellous system set by Allah has put together in human structure. Taken this way, the word *amshāj* allays the greatest doubt of the rejecters of Resurrection. Their main objection was that once dead and reduced to crumbled bones and dust, they could not be raised again; they thought this impossible. The answer: at the inception, man was composed of particles and elements from all parts of the world. **Allah did not find this difficult the first time — why should He find its recreation difficult the second time?**

**"Then man changes,"** says Ibn Kathīr, "from stage to stage, condition to condition and color to color."

**Nabtalīhi — "in order to try him."** Ibn Kathīr glosses it simply: *We test him*, and cites the parallel, "That He may test you which of you is best in deed" (67:2). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes the verb derives from **ibtilāʼ**, "to put to test", and says this phrase puts forward the **wisdom underlying human creation**: Allah has created man to put him to a test — a test defined in the verses that follow.

**"So, We made him hearer and seer."** Ibn Kathīr's comment is worth sitting with: *We gave him the faculties of hearing and sight so that he would be able to use them for obedience and disobedience.* The same ear, the same eye, can carry a man either way.

## Ayah 3: shown the road — grateful or ungrateful

**"Verily, We guided him to the way, whether he be grateful or ungrateful."**

**What "guided" means here.** Ibn Kathīr defines it precisely: *We explained it to him, made it clear to him and showed it to him.* He supports this with two parallels:

- "And as for Thamūd, **We guided them** but they preferred blindness to guidance" (41:17).
- "And We guided him to the two ways" (90:10), meaning, says Ibn Kathīr, *We explained to him the path of good and the path of evil* — the statement of ʿIkrimah, ʿAṭiyah, Ibn Zayd, and Mujāhid from what is well known from him, and of the majority.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān fills in how the showing happened: **Allah sent Prophets and celestial Books** for the purpose of showing man both ways, one leading to Paradise and the other to Hell, and man has been given a choice to adopt either one. No one is asked to find the way in the dark.

**Grateful or ungrateful — the two groups.** This, says Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, led mankind into two groups: the first of those who, appreciating Allah's bounties, offered gratitude to Allah and believed in Him; the second of those who remained ungrateful to Allah's favours and disbelieved. Notice how the commentary pairs them — gratitude stands with belief, and ingratitude with disbelief.

On "whether he be grateful or ungrateful," Ibn Kathīr says: *This is his decree. Thus, with this he is either wretched or happy.* He then cites a hadith recorded by **Muslim** from Abū Mālik al-Ashʿarī, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:

> "All of mankind wakes up in the morning the merchant of his own soul. So he either imprisons it or sets it free."

Every morning you open a shop. The only stock you have is yourself, and by the end of the day you have traded it into either bondage or freedom.

## Ayah 4: what has already been prepared

**"Verily, We have prepared for the disbelievers iron chains, iron collars, and Saʿīr."**

Ibn Kathīr says Allah informs us of **what He has waiting** for those of His creatures who disbelieve in Him: chains, iron collars, and **Saʿīr** — which is, he says, *the flame and fire of Hell*. He sets beside it: "When iron collars will be rounded over their necks, and the chains, they shall be dragged along, in the boiling water, then they will be burned in the Fire" (40:71–72). The order is there in the ayah itself: the collar at the neck, the chain for the dragging, then the boiling water, then the Fire.

The force of the ayah lies in its verb — **aʿtadnā**, *We have prepared*. What is described is not left vague for later; it is already made ready.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sets out the structure directly: after the description of the two groups, the next verse describes the punishment and evil consequences of the disbelievers — shackles, iron-collars and a blazing Fire — while on the other hand, huge bounties are mentioned for the believers and the righteous. Of those bounties, drinkables are mentioned first: from ayah 5, a drink from a goblet blended with camphor.

## Living it

- **Reflect backwards until it changes you.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes reflection on your own former non-mention the road to discovering your own reality, and to complete faith and unshaken belief in Allah, His Omniscience and His Omnipotence. Its own example is an ordinary person of seventy, simply thinking back.
- **Guard the two faculties.** Ibn Kathīr says hearing and sight were given "so that he would be able to use them for obedience and disobedience." What passes through your ears and eyes is the equipment of the test named in ayah 2.
- **Be in the first group.** In Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's description, the grateful are those who appreciated Allah's bounties and believed; the ungrateful are those who remained ungrateful to His favours and disbelieved.
- **Trade well this morning.** The hadith recorded by Muslim from Abū Mālik al-Ashʿarī puts it into a single day: you are the merchant of your own soul, and you either imprison it or set it free.

passages.title: The righteous: the cup of Kāfūr, their deeds, their reward
passages.tafsir:
**What this passage is.** Ayah 4 has just named what waits for those who reject Allah: chains, iron collars, and *Saʿīr* — which Ibn Kathir explains as the flame and fire of Hell, setting beside it Allah's words, "When iron collars will be rounded over their necks, and the chains, they shall be dragged along, in the boiling water, then they will be burned in the Fire" (40:71–72). Ayat 5–12 are the answering half of that picture: people who are handed a cup instead of chains and dressed in silk instead of collars.

What holds the eight ayat together is their shape. The reward comes first (5–6), the deeds that earned it come second (7–10), and the reward returns at the end, enlarged and explained (11–12). Allah shows us the destination, walks us back down the road that leads to it, then sets us at the destination again. And notice how modest that road is. No grand achievement is named — only keeping a promise, fearing a Day, feeding someone hungry, and saying nothing about it afterwards.

## The cup and the spring (ayat 5–6)

*Al-Abrār* — the virtuous, the righteous — "shall drink of a cup mixed with Kāfūr." **Kāfūr** is camphor, and Ibn Kathir says its properties are well known: it is cooling, and it carries a nice fragrance. To that he adds the thing this world's camphor lacks — in Paradise its taste will be delicious. Al-Hasan said, "The coolness of the camphor will be in the pleasantness of ginger."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes the same point protectively, and it is worth pausing on, because a reader who knows camphor from a chemist's shelf may be baffled: if the word is taken in its popular sense, that does not necessarily signify that the camphor of Paradise is to be equated with the camphor available in this world, because the latter is not palatable. What the Qurʼān is naming is coolness and fragrance — the qualities — not the substance on the shelf.

**Is Kāfūr a flavour or a place?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that some commentators say Kāfūr refers to a fountain in Paradise, and that ayah 6 settles the question grammatically. In ayah 6, *ʿaynan* ("a spring") is a *badal* — a complement, a noun placed alongside an earlier word to explain what it actually refers to — for *kāfūran*. Given that construction, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says, it becomes certain that Kāfūr is the name of a spring, and that in order to enhance the taste and pleasure of this drink it will be mixed with water from it. But Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives the alternative fairly: if *ʿaynan* is instead taken as an explanation of *kaʼs* (the goblet), the meaning is that the goblet will contain a drink from a spring specified for "Allah's slaves" — and in that case it is also possible that "Allah's slaves" refers to a category other than the *Abrār*.

Ibn Kathir draws a careful distinction between two ways of drinking: the drink that will be mixed for these righteous people is *taken from* Kāfūr, while Kāfūr is a spring that Allah's close servants will drink from **directly, without it being mixed with anything**, and they will drink to their fill from it. He notes a fine point of the Arabic here — the verb *yashrabu*, "to drink," includes within it the meaning of *yarwā*, to have one's thirst quenched. This is not sipping. It is thirst ended.

**"Causing it to gush forth abundantly."** *Yufajjirūnahā tafjīran.* *At-Tafjīr*, Ibn Kathir explains, means to cause to gush forth or flow out — the same word used when the deniers said, "We shall not believe in you until you cause a spring to gush forth from the earth for us" (17:90), and again where Allah says, "We caused a river to gush forth in the midst of them" (18:33).

The startling thing is the subject of the verb: *they* make it gush. Mujahid said this means they will divert it to wherever they wish; ʿIkrimah and Qatadah both made similar statements, and ath-Thawrī said, "They will cause it to flow wherever they wish." Ibn Kathir draws out the picture: they will have control of it however and wherever they wish, with access to it from their castles, their homes, their sitting rooms and their residences. In this world the thirsty go to the water. There, the water goes where the servant of Allah points.

## The deeds behind the cup (ayat 7–10)

Now the Qurʼān turns and shows us why. Ibn Kathir titles this section simply "The Deeds of these Righteous People," and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads ayah 7 and ayah 8 as giving the two reasons these favours will be apportioned to them.

### They keep their word (ayah 7)

"They fulfil their vows." A *nadhr*, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains, literally means "to take upon oneself an obligation which Sharīʿah has not obligated on him" — and once a vow is taken, it becomes obligatory to fulfil it. That is the whole logic of the ayah, and it is an argument from the smaller to the greater: when they are so particular about fulfilling vows they took upon themselves, they would be even more particular about fulfilling the obligations enjoined upon them by Allah. So "the fulfilment of vows" here covers the entire spectrum of religious obligations. Ibn Kathir says the same from the other end: they devote themselves to worshipping Allah through what He made obligatory upon them, and they worship Him by fulfilling their vows as well.

**From the Sunnah.** Imam Malik reported from Talhah bin ʿAbdul-Malik al-Aylī, who reported from al-Qāsim bin Malik, from ʿĀʼishah, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Whoever makes a vow to obey Allah, then he should obey Him. And whoever makes a vow to disobey Allah, then he should not disobey Him." Ibn Kathir notes that al-Bukhari also recorded this hadith from Malik.

**A ruling worth knowing.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān lists the conditions that must be met before a vow can be constituted at all. (1) The vow must be legitimate and permissible — not a sin. (2) It must not be something Allah has already legislated as an obligatory duty; if a person were to vow that he will perform the prescribed prayer or the witr prayer, the vow would be null and void, because it is already a prescribed obligation. (3) According to Imam Aʿẓam Abū Ḥanīfah, it is also a condition that the vowed act be an act of worship in itself, and one belonging to those forms of worship that have been made obligatory in some way or the other — prayers, fasting, charity, sacrifice and so on. So a vow to pay a visit to a sick patient or to follow a funeral procession is not a valid vow: those acts carry reward, but they are not acts of worship in themselves (*al-ʿibādāt ul-maqṣūdah*, "worship that is an end in itself"). Detailed rules on this belong to the books of jurisprudence.

Mufti Muhammad Taqi Usmani adds a clarifying footnote, because a layman easily confuses a vow with an oath. If a person makes a vow to commit a sin — telling a lie, drinking liquor — that vow is not recognised by the Sharīʿah: he must abstain from the sin, and since the vow is not recognised, no expiation (*kaffārah*) is needed. The rule about *oaths* is different: someone who swears an oath to tell a lie has to break the oath and offer expiation.

### And they fear a Day (ayah 7)

The second half of ayah 7 keeps them honest: "they fear a Day whose evil will be wide-spreading." Ibn Kathir says these people also abandon the forbidden things Allah has prohibited for them, out of fear of an evil reckoning on the Day of Return. The word is *mustaṭīran*; Ibn ʿAbbas glossed it in a single word, "Spreading." Qatadah said, "By Allah! The evil of that Day will spread until it fills the heavens and the earth." It is the Day when the evil will spread out among all people — except for those upon whom Allah has had mercy.

So both wings are present. Obedience out of devotion, restraint out of fear.

### They give food they want themselves (ayah 8)

"And they give food, in spite of their love for it, to the poor, the orphan and the captive."

Everything turns on *ʿalā ḥubbihi* — "in spite of their love for it." Whose love, and for what? Ibn Kathir reports that it has been said this means the love of Allah, the pronoun referring to Allah. However, he judges the most apparent meaning to be that the pronoun refers to **the food**: they give food while they themselves love it and desire it. This was stated by Mujahid and Muqātil, and it was the preferred opinion of Ibn Jarir. It matches Allah's other words, "And gives his wealth, in spite of love for it" (2:177), and "By no means shall you attain al-Birr unless you spend of that which you love" (3:92). And it matches a hadith Ibn Kathir cites as being in the Ṣaḥīḥ: "The best charity is that which you give while you are healthy, covetous, hoping for wealth and fearing poverty" — meaning, he explains, in the condition of your love for wealth, your eagerness for it and your need for it.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān presses the point to where it stings: they give food to the needy while they themselves love it and desire it — **not** that they eat to their fill and give the left-over food to the needy and poor.

**The captive.** The third recipient is the one that stops a modern reader. Ibn Kathir reports a genuine spread of views. Saʿīd bin Jubayr, al-Hasan and aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk all said the captive is the captive among the people of the Qiblah — that is, the Muslims. Ibn ʿAbbas said that at the time this ayah was revealed, the Muslims' captives were idolaters. The proof he points to is from the day of Badr: the Messenger of Allah ﷺ commanded his Companions to treat the captives respectfully, and they would give them preference over themselves when eating their meals — feeding the enemy first and going short. ʿIkrimah said the captives are the slaves, and Ibn Jarir preferred this opinion, since the ayah generally refers to both the Muslim and the idolaters; Saʿīd bin Jubayr, ʿAṭāʼ, al-Hasan and Qatadah all made similar statements, and Mujahid said simply, "He is the prisoner."

Ibn Kathir adds that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ advised treating servants well in more than one hadith, and that this held such importance with him that the last statement of advice he gave before dying was his saying: "The prayer (As-Salah) and what your right hand possesses (slaves)."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān carries the ruling forward to any Muslim society: "captive" refers to all prisoners — Muslim criminals as well as non-Muslims who are kept in prisons according to the principles of the Sharīʿah. It is the responsibility of the Islamic government to feed them, so anyone who feeds them is actually assisting the government and the public treasury, and feeding prisoners, even non-Muslim ones, is an act of reward. In the early days of Islam especially, feeding the prisoners and taking care of them was a responsibility shared by the general body of Muslims — as it happened with the prisoners of the Battle of Badr.

Read the three together and you see the shape of the mercy being praised: the *poor* have nothing, the *orphan* has no one, the *captive* has no freedom. Not one of them can pay you back.

### The sentence nobody hears (ayat 9–10)

"We feed you seeking Allah's Face only. We wish for no reward, nor thanks from you." Ibn Kathir glosses "seeking Allah's Face" as hoping for the reward of Allah and His pleasure. Then he unpacks the second clause in two directions: *we do not seek any reward from you in return for it, and we are not seeking for you to thank us in front of the people.* Both the cash and the credit are refused.

Here comes the most beautiful comment in the whole passage. Mujahid and Saʿīd bin Jubayr both said: "By Allah! They do not say this with their tongues, but rather, Allah knows it in their hearts and He commends them for it. Every seeker should seek after this." The words of ayah 9 were never spoken aloud. Allah heard them anyway, and then published them in His Book. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān echoes the wonder of it: neither were they there, nor was there any demand from them — it is only Allah's mercy that listened to what they never said.

That is the standard being set. Not merely charity without a receipt, but charity without a sentence — and Allah records the sentence for you.

**"A Day that is ʿAbūs and Qamṭarīr."** Ayah 10 gives their motive, and Ibn Kathir renders it as: we only do this so that perhaps Allah may have mercy on us and treat us with gentleness on that Day. The two words are almost untranslatable, and the early scholars circled them from different sides. ʿAlī bin Abī Ṭalḥah reported from Ibn ʿAbbas: *ʿAbūs* means difficult, *Qamṭarīr* means long. ʿIkrimah and others said from Ibn ʿAbbas that the disbeliever will frown on that Day until sweat will flow between his eyes like tar. Mujahid said *ʿAbūs* means frowning with the two lips and *Qamṭarīr* means drawing up the face in a scowl. Saʿīd bin Jubayr and Qatadah said, "Faces will be made to frown due to dismay," *Qamṭarīr* being the contraction of the forehead and what is between the two eyes due to dismay. Ibn Zayd said *ʿAbūs* is the evil and *Qamṭarīr* is the severity.

Put together, the Day is being described by the face it produces. It is a Day so hard and so long that you can read it off a person's forehead.

## What Allah gave them (ayat 11–12)

"So Allah saved them from the evil of that Day, and gave them *Naḍrah* and joy." Ibn Kathir notes that this is used as a way of eloquence in stating similarity — the two halves are made to match. They *feared* the evil of that Day (ayah 7, ayah 10), so — as Ibn Kathir puts it — He protects them from that which they fear of it.

**Naḍrah and surūr.** Ibn Kathir separates the two precisely: *Naḍrah* — a light of beauty — is in their **faces**, and *surūr* — joy — is in their **hearts**. Al-Hasan al-Baṣrī, Qatadah, Abū ʿĀliyah and ar-Rabīʿ bin Anas all stated this. It is the state Allah describes elsewhere: "Some faces that Day will be bright, laughing, rejoicing at good news" (80:38–39). And Ibn Kathir explains the link between the two: if the heart is happy, then the face will be enlightened. He illustrates it from the Prophet ﷺ himself — Kaʿb bin Malik said, in his lengthy hadith, that whenever the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was happy his face would be radiant until it was as if it were a piece of the moon; and ʿĀʼishah said, "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ entered into my home happy and his facial expression was glowing."

Weigh the contrast the sūrah has built. On that Day one set of faces is contracted between the eyes with dismay, sweat running like tar; another set is lit from inside because the heart behind it is safe.

**"And their recompense, because they were patient, is Paradise and silken garments."** Ibn Kathir reads ayah 12 as: due to their patience He will give them, bestow upon them and accommodate them with Paradise and silken garments — meaning a home that is spacious, a delightful life, and fine clothing. Set this against ayah 4 and the sūrah's design is complete: iron collars there, silk here.

And why patience, when the deeds listed were vows and feeding? Al-Ḥāfiẓ Ibn ʿAsākir said, in his biography of Hishām bin Sulaymān ad-Dārānī, that Sūrat al-Insān was recited to Abū Sulaymān ad-Dārānī, and when the reciter reached "And their recompense shall be Paradise, and silken garments, because they were patient," he said: **"Because they were patient in leaving off their desires in the world."** That is the thread. Giving away food you wanted, refusing the thanks you were owed, honouring a vow when it became inconvenient — every deed in ayat 7–10 is an act of saying no to yourself. The Qurʼān gathers them all under one word: *ṣabr*.

## Living it

The passage is unusually concrete, so what it asks is concrete too.

**Give what you would have enjoyed.** Not the surplus, not the left-overs — Maʿārif ul Qurʼān rules that reading out explicitly. The measure of the gift is what it cost your own appetite.

**Choose recipients who cannot repay you.** The poor, the orphan, the captive: three people with nothing to give back. The prisoner in particular — Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that feeding prisoners is an act of reward even when they are not Muslims.

**Then say nothing.** No reward sought, no thanks sought, not even the quiet satisfaction of being seen to have given. Mujahid and Saʿīd bin Jubayr said the *Abrār* never even said the words with their tongues — and then added the line every reader should take personally: *every seeker should seek after this.*

**Keep the promises you made to Allah.** If a vow was valid, fulfil it. And take the lesson Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws from the ayah: someone so particular about an obligation he took upon himself would be even more particular about the obligations Allah enjoined upon him.

passages.title: Inside the promised Garden: shade, Salsabīl, and silk
passages.tafsir:
**The passage in one breath.** These ten ayat take you inside the Garden and keep you there. Having promised the reward in general terms, the sūrah now walks slowly through it: the seat you are sitting on, the air on your skin, the branch over your head, the cup in your hand, the servants moving around you, the clothes on your back — and only at the very end, in ayah 22, does a voice finally speak and tell you why any of it is yours.

**What holds them together.** Two threads. First, in every single image the blessing moves toward the person, and the person never reaches, strains, or waits. Shade rests close over them, fruit comes down, vessels are carried round, drink is given, servants circulate. The people of the Garden are at rest — *muttakiʾīn*, "reclining" (ayah 13) — while everything else is in motion for their sake. Second, all of it is framed as **repayment**. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points back to ayah 8, where these same people fed the needy, the orphan and the captive *despite their love for it*, and says plainly that this is the reason the inmates of Paradise receive these favours. Ayah 22 closes that loop out loud.

## Ayah 13 — a place with no weather

*Muttakiʾīn fīhā ʿalā al-arāʾik* — "reclining therein on raised couches." Ibn Kathir notes that there is a difference of opinion over exactly what this reclining is: lying down, reclining on the elbows, sitting down cross-legged, or being firmly seated. What all four share is the posture of someone who has arrived and has nothing left to do. As for *al-arāʾik*, he explains them as couches beneath curtained canopies — not bare benches but furnished, sheltered, honoured seating.

Then: *lā yarawna fīhā shamsan wa lā zamharīrā* — "they will see there neither the excessive heat, nor the excessive bitter cold." Ibn Kathir's gloss deserves slow reading: **there will be no disturbing heat with them, nor any painful cold, rather there will only be one climate that will be always and eternal and they will not want it to be changed.**

Notice the pairing in the ayah itself: the two ends of physical misery, burning heat and biting cold, both simply absent. But that last clause of Ibn Kathir is the remarkable one. In this world comfort is restless — we are forever adjusting. There the condition is fixed *and* the wish to change it is gone: the blessing lies as much in the contentment as in the climate.

## Ayah 14 — shade that leans in, fruit that comes down

*Wa dāniyatan ʿalayhim ẓilāluhā* — "and the shade thereof is close upon them." Ibn Kathir explains simply: the branches will be close to them. Not shade you walk to find, but shade already resting over you.

Then the extraordinary phrase: *wa dhullilat quṭūfuhā tadhlīlā* — "and the bunches of fruit thereof will hang low within their reach." Ibn Kathir explains it this way: whenever he attempts to get any fruit, it will come nearer to him and come down from its highest branch **as if it hears and obeys**.

Mujahid drew this out with a picture you will not forget: *"If he stands it will rise with him an equal amount, if he sits it will lower itself for him so that he can reach it and if he lies down it will lower itself for him more so that he can reach it."* He then anchors the whole image on the single word *tadhlīlan*. The tree tracks the man. And Qatadah adds the detail that removes the last friction of orchard life: *"No thorn or distance will repel their hands away from it."*

Ibn Kathir links this to two other ayat saying the same thing from different angles — *"And fruits of the two gardens will be near at hand"* (55:54) and *"The fruits in bunches whereof will be low and near at hand"* (69:23).

## Ayat 15–16 — silver you can see through

*Wa yuṭāfu ʿalayhim bi-āniyatin min fiḍḍatin wa akwāb* — "and among them will be passed round vessels of silver and cups." Ibn Kathir: servants will go around them with containers of food made of silver and cups of drink. He notes the precise sense of *akwāb*: **these are drinking vessels that do not have handles or spouts.**

Then comes one of the most quietly astonishing descriptions in the Qurʾān: *qawārīra min fiḍḍah* — "crystal-clear, made of silver." Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujahid, al-Hasan al-Basri and others have all said the same thing: *"It is the whiteness of silver in the transparency of glass."* Ibn Kathir then presses the point: *qawārīr* is only made of glass — so these cups are genuinely **made of silver**, but due to their fine thinness, what is inside of them will be visible from outside of them, as if they were glass. He concludes: this is among the things of which there is nothing like in this world.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sharpens the paradox: silver vessels in this world are dense and can never be like glass, and what is made of glass can never be silver — here they are two contradictory concepts. It is a characteristic of Paradise that its glasses will be as bright as silver, and as transparent and sparkling as crystal. And it records from Sayyidnā Ibn ʿAbbās that the blessings given in Paradise have their likes in this world also, **except** these vessels, which are made of silver but as transparent as a mirror.

*Qaddarūhā taqdīrā* — "they will determine the measure thereof." Ibn Kathir explains it as the amount that will quench their thirst: **it will not be more than that nor less than it**, rather it will be prepared in an amount that is suitable for quenching the thirst of their drinkers. He reports this as the position of a long line of early authorities — Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujahid, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, Abū Ṣāliḥ, Qatādah, Ibn Abzā, ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr, ash-Shaʿbī and Ibn Zayd — as stated by Ibn Jarīr and others. Ibn Kathir calls this the most excellent provision, distinction and honour.

That is honour, not restriction. Here abundance and precision pull against each other — too much, or too little — while there every cup arrives already fitted to the one who will drink it.

## Ayat 17–18 — the hot cup, and the spring called Salsabīl

*Wa yusqawna fīhā kaʾsan kāna mizājuhā zanjabīlā* — "and they will be given to drink there of a cup mixed with *zanjabīl* (ginger)." Ibn Kathir says this is given to the righteous, and glosses *kaʾs* as a drink of wine. He reads the ginger against the camphor mentioned earlier in the sūrah: **on one occasion they will be given a drink that is mixed with camphor, and it is cool; then on another occasion they will be given a drink mixed with ginger, and it is hot — so that their affair will be balanced.** Even the pleasures alternate with a kind of wisdom.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds the cultural key: the Arabs loved that their drink should be mixed with ginger, so it is mentioned here in the context of Paradise — served, of course, with a quality and splendour belonging to Paradise. And it records the principle some scholars state: the only thing the blessings of Paradise and the blessings of this world share in common is their *name*, and they have nothing else in common. The ginger of this world cannot be equated with the ginger of Paradise. That principle should govern how you read this entire passage — every noun in it is a familiar word pointing at an unfamiliar reality.

Ibn Kathir also notes a distinction running quietly through these ayat. The cup mixed with ginger is described for **the righteous**; as for **those who are nearest to Allah**, Qatādah and others said they will drink from all of it however they wish. Earlier in the sūrah, ayah 6 called that source *"a spring wherefrom the servants of Allah will drink."*

*ʿAynan fīhā tusammā Salsabīlā* — "a spring there, called Salsabīl." ʿIkrimah said it is the name of a spring in Paradise. Mujahid explained the name itself: **it is called this due to its continuous flowing and the severity of its current.** A spring that does not pool and stagnate but runs, keeps running, and runs strongly.

## Ayah 19 — servers like scattered pearls

*Wa yaṭūfu ʿalayhim wildānun mukhalladūn* — "and round about them will serve boys of everlasting youth." Ibn Kathir: young boys from the boys of Paradise will go around serving the people of Paradise. *Mukhalladūn* means **in one state forever which they will never be changing from; they will not increase in age** — no ageing, no fading, no growing out of that freshness. (He notes that those who have described them as wearing earrings in their ears interpreted the meaning that way because a child is befitting of this description and not an adult man.)

*Idhā raʾaytahum ḥasibtahum luʾluʾan manthūrā* — "if you see them, you would think them scattered pearls." Ibn Kathir unfolds the comparison: when you see them dispersing to fulfil the needs of their masters — their great number, their beautiful faces, handsome colours, fine clothing and ornaments — you would think that they were scattered pearls. And he adds a judgement of taste: **there is no better quality than this, nor is there anything nicer to look at than scattered pearls in a beautiful place.**

## Ayah 20 — when you look

*Wa idhā raʾayta thamma raʾayta naʿīman wa mulkan kabīrā* — "and when you look there, you will see a delight, and a great dominion." Ibn Kathir reads the address as directed to the Prophet ﷺ — "when you see it, O Muhammad" — and *thamma* as simply "there": that is, Paradise, with its beauty, its vastness, its loftiness, and the joy and happiness it contains.

Every other ayah in this passage hands you one specific thing to picture — a couch, a branch, a cup, a face. This one pulls the camera back and names the whole: *naʿīm* and *mulk kabīr*. Ibn Kathir's gloss on *mulkan kabīrā*: there will be a great kingdom that belongs to Allah, and a dazzling, splendid dominion.

To convey the scale, Ibn Kathir cites what has been **confirmed in the Sahih**: that Allah will say to the last of the people of the Fire to be taken out of it, and the last of the people to enter into Paradise, *"verily, you will have similar to the world and ten worlds like it (in addition to it)."* Then he asks the question that does the real work: if this is what He will give to the least of those who will be in Paradise, then what do you think about the one who will have a higher status and will be favoured even more by Allah?

## Ayah 21 — silk outside, and a drink that cleans the inside

*ʿĀliyahum thiyābu sundusin khuḍrun wa istabraq* — "their garments will be of fine green silk, and *istabraq*." Ibn Kathir distinguishes the two fabrics: *sundus* is a high quality silk, and these garments will be shirts and similar clothing from the undergarments; as for *istabraq* — which he glosses as velvet — some of it has a glitter and shimmer to it, and it is that which is worn as **outer** clothes, just as is well known in clothing. Inner layer and outer layer, exactly as garments are worn in ordinary life.

*Wa ḥullū asāwira min fiḍḍah* — "and they will be adorned with bracelets of silver." Ibn Kathir marks this as a description of **the righteous**; as for those who will be near to Allah, their description is as Allah says: *"wherein they will be adorned with bracelets of gold and pearls and their garments therein will be of silk"* (22:23) — the same distinction of ranks we met at the cup.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān handles two natural questions here. *Asāwir* is the plural of *siwār*, a bracelet worn around the wrist. First, is there a discrepancy between silver bracelets in this ayah and gold in 22:23? No — sometimes the silver bracelets will be worn and at other times the gold, or some will wear gold and others will wear silver. Second, and more interesting for a modern reader: a bracelet looks good on women but does not suit men; why will the men of Paradise wear them? The answer given is that the suitability of any piece of jewellery to men or women depends on **custom**, and the style and appeal of jewellery differ from country to country and vary from nation to nation — in some cultures a piece is treated as highly inappropriate for men, and in others it is regarded as highly beautiful and elegant. The Chosroes, the Persian kings, used to wear bracelets around their wrists, with various kinds of jewellery studded on their chest and crown, counted as a distinctive feature of their prestige and honour; after the conquest of the Persian empire, the treasures that fell into Muslim hands contained the Persian Emperor's bracelets. If taste varies that much within this world, our taste here cannot be used to measure theirs there.

Then the ayah turns from the surface to the depths: *wa saqāhum rabbuhum sharāban ṭahūrā* — "and their Lord will give them a purifying drink." Ibn Kathir: it will **purify their insides** of envy, despise, hatred, harm and the other reprehensible character traits. And note the wording of the ayah itself. Elsewhere in the passage the vessels are carried round by servants; this drink is attributed to *rabbuhum*, "their Lord" — the honour is in the Giver, not only in the gift.

Ibn Kathir records from the Commander of the believers, ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, that he said: when the people of Paradise come to the Gate of Paradise, they will find two springs there; then it will be as if they were inspired with what to do, so they will drink from one of them and Allah will remove whatever harmfulness there may be within them; then they will bathe in the other spring and a glow of delight will run all over them. Thus, as Ibn Kathir puts it, Allah informs of their outward condition and their inner beauty.

That is the pattern of the whole ayah, and the answer to anyone who thinks this passage is only about luxury: silk and silver on the outside, a heart washed clean of envy and hatred on the inside. Paradise is not merely a better place; its people are made better people.

## Ayah 22 — the sentence that explains the other nine

*Inna hādhā kāna lakum jazāʾan wa kāna saʿyukum mashkūrā* — "verily, this is a reward for you, and your endeavour has been accepted." Ibn Kathir says this will be said to them **in honour of them and as a goodness towards them**, and he places it alongside *"Eat and drink at ease for that which you have sent forth before you in days past!"* (69:24) and *"And it will be cried out to them: this is the Paradise which you have inherited for what you used to do"* (7:43). On *mashkūrā* he comments: Allah the Exalted will reward you for a small amount of deeds with a large amount of reward.

Sit with how the two sources render that final word. Ibn Kathir's translation reads *"your endeavour has been accepted"*; Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's reads *"your effort has been appreciated."* Between them they catch what is happening: the servant's small effort, offered in a short life, is not merely tolerated by the Lord of the worlds — it is received, and answered.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads these words as a **congratulation**: Allah will address the inmates of Paradise once they have entered it, and will announce to them that these amazing bounties are granted as a reward for the good deeds they had done in the world, and that their deeds have been appreciated by Allah. It adds a line worth carrying: for the people of love, the Divine congratulatory expressions will outweigh all the other blessings of Paradise put together — because the congratulatory words are a proof positive of Divine pleasure.

That is the point of the whole passage. The couches, the shade, the silver, Salsabīl, the pearls, the silk — all of it is real, and all of it is secondary. The summit is being told, by Allah Himself, *well done*.

## Living it

**The deed behind the Garden.** Do not read ayat 13–22 apart from ayah 8. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is explicit that the other reason the inmates of Paradise receive these favours is their feeding of the needy, the orphans and the captives — and that *ʿalā ḥubbihi*, "despite their love for it," means they give food to the needy while they themselves love it and desire it, **not** that they eat to their fill and give the left-over food to the needy and poor. The Garden of reclining is the return on food given away while still wanting it.

**And the captive.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān takes *asīr* broadly: the word refers to all prisoners — Muslim criminals as well as non-Muslims kept in prisons according to the principles of the Sharīʿah. It is the responsibility of the Islamic government to feed them, so anyone who feeds them is in effect assisting the government and the public treasury; therefore feeding prisoners, even non-Muslims, is an act of reward. In the early days of Islam especially, feeding the prisoners and taking care of them or protecting them was a responsibility shared by the general body of Muslims, as it happened with the prisoners of the Battle of Badr. Note where the generosity of this sūrah reaches: to the people with the least social claim on it.

**How to hold the imagery.** Read "silk," "ginger," "silver," "spring," and let each word point past itself — Maʿārif ul Qurʼān has already told you that the blessings of the two worlds may share nothing but a name. The silver cup you can see through is the sūrah's own proof that you are not being shown a better version of this world; you are being shown something else entirely, described in the only vocabulary you have.

passages.title: The Prophet's charge: endure the deniers, worship through the night
passages.tafsir:
**What this passage is.** Having spent the surah describing the righteous and the Paradise prepared for them, Allah now turns and speaks directly to His Messenger ﷺ. Ayah 23 names the gift he has been given; ayat 24–26 name what that gift asks of him — patience, refusal to bend, and worship at both ends of the day and into the night; ayat 27–28 explain why the people opposing him are the way they are, and what Allah says about the frames those people were given.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the seam clearly. After the general blessings of the inmates of Paradise have been mentioned, "special blessings that are conferred on the Holy Prophet are listed": first "the blessing in the form of the revelation of the Qur'an"; then the direction that "the opponents and obdurate non-believers will obstinately reject the message and persecute him. So, he is to submit patiently to Allah's decision, and he should not obey any sinner or ungrateful person"; and then, "secondly, he is commanded to pronounce the name of Allah, and worship Him day and night."

## Ayah 23 — the gift named before the burden

**"Indeed, it is We Who have revealed the Quran to you ˹O Prophet˺."**

Ibn Kathir's comment here is a single sentence, and it sets up everything that follows: "Allah reminds His Messenger ﷺ of how He blessed him by revealing the Magnificent Qur'an to him."

The rendering carried in Ibn Kathir's own text reads, "Verily, it is We Who have sent down the Qur'an to you by stages." Whatever else this passage is going to ask of the Prophet ﷺ, it opens by naming what he has already been given.

That order matters. Allah does not open with *endure the deniers*. He opens with the blessing — and, as we are about to see, Ibn Kathir makes that sequence explicit when he reaches the next ayah.

## Ayah 24 — patience, and the refusal to bend

**"Therefore be patient with constancy to the command of your Lord, and obey neither a sinner nor a disbeliever among them."**

Ibn Kathir ties this command directly back to the gift just named: "just as you have been honored by what has been revealed to you, then be patient with His decree and decision and know that He will handle your affairs in a good manner."

Read that twice. The patience being asked for is not gritted-teeth endurance of a situation that has gone wrong. It is patience with the decree of the One who — Ibn Kathir adds in the same breath — "will handle your affairs in a good manner." The same Lord who sent down the Book is the One whose decision he is waiting on. A promise is attached to the command; it is not merely a demand.

**"And obey neither a sinner (Athim) nor a disbeliever (Kafur) among them."** Ibn Kathir gives each of the two words a precise sense: "The Athim is the sinner in his deeds and the Kafur is the disbeliever in his heart." So the pairing is not decoration. One names corruption that shows on the outside, in a person's conduct; the other names denial that sits inside, in the heart.

And what exactly is forbidden? Ibn Kathir: "do not obey the disbelievers and the hypocrites if they wish to deter you from what has been revealed to you. Rather convey that which has been revealed to you from your Lord and put your trust in Allah, for verily, Allah will protect you from the people."

This is the heart of it. The prohibition is specifically about obedience in the matter of the message — obeying those who "wish to deter you from what has been revealed to you." And Ibn Kathir's alternative to yielding is not silence. It is to keep conveying, with trust placed in Allah, and with the safety a person might have hoped to buy by softening the message already guaranteed from another direction: "Allah will protect you from the people."

## Ayat 25–26 — the daily and nightly discipline

Three commands follow, and together they cover the whole cycle of a day.

**"And remember the Name of your Lord every morning and afternoon" (25).** Ibn Kathir's gloss is deliberately simple: "at the beginning of the day and at its end." The day is bracketed at both ends by the remembrance of Allah's Name, so that whatever fills the middle — including hostility — is enclosed by something else.

**"And during the night, prostrate yourself to Him" (26a).** The translation given for this ayah reads "prostrate before Him during part of the night," and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān lists it among the commands laid on him: "he should prostrate before Him, during the night."

**"...and glorify Him a long night through" (26b).** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān describes this as being commanded to "pronounce His purity for long times at night." It is a fitting answer to a day spent under rejection.

Ibn Kathir places this alongside two other passages. First: "And in some parts of the night offer the Salah with it (the Qur'an), as an additional prayer (Tahajjud) for you. It may be that your Lord will raise you to Maqam Mahmud" (17:79) — night prayer set beside a promise, though Ibn Kathir's text here leaves the term *Maqam Mahmud* untranslated. Second, the opening of Sūrat al-Muzzammil: "O you wrapped! Stand all night, except a little. Half of it or a little less than that, or a little more. And recite the Qur'an Tartil" (73:1–4) — the same charge of night standing and recitation, laid on the Prophet ﷺ in another place.

**Why worship is the prescription.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān states the point directly: this preoccupation "will serve as a remedy for the non-believers' persecution." That is a striking claim and worth sitting with. When a person is opposed, the instinctive remedies are argument, avoidance, or retaliation. What is prescribed to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ is remembrance, prostration, and a long night of glorifying Him. The hostility is not answered on its own terms at all.

## Ayah 27 — the diagnosis

**"Verily, these love the present life of this world, and put behind them a heavy Day."**

Ibn Kathir: "Allah reprimands the disbelievers and those similar to them who love the world and are devoted and dedicated to it, who put the abode of the Hereafter behind them in disregard." The phrase "and those similar to them" is important — the reprimand is not sealed off around one set of opponents. The "heavy Day," Ibn Kathir says, means "the Day of Judgement."

The two halves of the ayah picture a bad trade. What they love is *al-ʿājilah* — the word Ibn Kathir renders "the present life of this world" and the translation renders "this fleeting world": the thing that is available right now. What they discard is heavy — and they put it *behind* them, which Ibn Kathir describes as putting the abode of the Hereafter behind them "in disregard," out of sight, where a person puts what he does not want to think about.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān offers this as the actual explanation for the opponents' stubbornness: the passage "shows the reason for the persistence of the obdurate infidels," namely that they "are intoxicated with the fleeting pleasures of this world, and have neglected the Hereafter." The cause is located not in the message but in the listener. The Prophet ﷺ, told to endure them, is being told what he is really up against.

## Ayah 28 — the evidence they are standing in

**"It is We Who created them, and We have made them of strong build."**

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points out what the ayah is doing: "if they had pondered in their own being or existence, they would have recognised and understood their Creator and Maker." The argument does not send them to the horizons; it sends them to their own bodies.

On the phrase rendered "We have made them of strong build," Ibn Kathir reports that "Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and others have said, 'This means their creation.'" Maʿārif ul Qurʼān renders the same phrase "have made their joints strong," and pauses on the wonder of it: though "man's limbs and organs are perpetually in motion, and the wear and tear on them is phenomenal, they continue to function from birth to death." Machines of iron or steel wear out and need regular servicing to keep running even a short while, while a body "made of soft tissues and muscles, functions for decades and scores of years without maintenance." Consider the joints of the fingers alone — "moved vigorously in different ways in an uncountable number of times," under heavy pressure and force, for seventy to eighty years on average, and still intact. "It is certainly only Allah Who makes this possible. 'Glorious is Allah, the Best of Creators!'"

**"And when We will, We can replace them with others like them with a complete replacement."** Here the commentary carries two readings, and Ibn Kathir reports both.

- **Ibn Kathir's own reading:** "when We wish, We will resurrect them on the Day of Judgement and change them, repeating their creation in a new form." He then draws the inference: "Here the beginning of their creation is a proof for the repetition of their creation." The One who assembled this frame the first time is able to assemble it again — so the heavy Day they have thrown behind them is no idle threat.
- **The reading of Ibn Zayd and Ibn Jarir:** "This means, if We wish We can bring another group of people besides them (in their place)." Ibn Kathir supports this sense with two parallels: "If He wills, He can take you away, O people, and bring others. And Allah is capable over that" (4:133), and "If He wills, He can remove you and bring a new creation! And for Allah that is not hard or difficult" (14:19–20).

Both readings land on the same reassurance for the Prophet ﷺ. Whether the meaning is *We will raise these very people again for the Reckoning* or *We can set them aside and bring another people entirely*, the deniers who look so immovable are, before Allah, entirely replaceable.

## Living it

- **Take the gift before the task.** The pattern of ayat 23–24 is the one Ibn Kathir spells out: "just as you have been honored by what has been revealed to you, then be patient." Hardship is meant to be carried by someone who remembers what he has been given.
- **Know what may not be conceded.** The command in ayah 24 is narrow and sharp: do not *obey* those who "wish to deter you from what has been revealed to you." And Ibn Kathir's answer to fear is not silence but reliance — convey it, and put your trust in Allah, "for verily, Allah will protect you from the people."
- **Bracket the day; give the night a portion.** Ayah 25 asks for the Name of your Lord "at the beginning of the day and at its end." Ayah 26 asks for prostration during part of the night and for glorifying Him a long night through. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's insight is that this is not an escape from opposition but the "remedy for the non-believers' persecution."
- **Watch for the trade in ayah 27.** Ibn Kathir extends the reprimand to "those similar to them." Loving what is immediate and pushing the heavy Day out of sight is not a disease confined to deniers.
- **Look at your own hands.** The proof offered in ayah 28 is nearer than any argument: joints that have carried you for decades without a single repair. And, as Ibn Kathir puts it, "the beginning of their creation is a proof for the repetition of their creation."

*(Ibn Kathir closes this passage with "This is the end of the Tafsir of Surat Al-Insan"; Maʿārif ul Qurʼān closes the same commentary as "Surah Ad-Dahr" — two names for the same surah.)*

passages.title: The reminder and the will of Allah
passages.tafsir:
**These three ayat close Sūrat al-Insān** — the sūrah also known as Sūrat ad-Dahr. They set two things beside each other and hold on to both: the Qur'an has been placed before you as a reminder, and whoever wills may take a path to his Lord — yet no one wills anything at all unless Allah wills.

One verb runs through all three ayat: *shāʾa*, "to will." In ayah 29 it is the human being's willing — *fa-man shāʾa*, "so whoever wills." In ayah 30 that willing is placed inside Allah's — "you cannot will, unless Allah wills." In ayah 31 the only willing named is His — "whom He wills." Ibn Kathir gathers this whole closing section under one heading: **"The Qur'an is a Reminder, and Guidance comes from the Help of Allah."** That heading is the passage in miniature.

## How the sūrah arrives here

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān traces the shape of the closing. Having mentioned the general blessings of the people of Paradise, the sūrah lists the special blessings conferred on the Prophet ﷺ — first among them the revelation of the Qur'an. He is then told that the obstinate rejecters will reject the message and persecute him, so he is to submit patiently to Allah's decision and to obey no sinner or ungrateful person. He is commanded to pronounce the Name of Allah and worship Him day and night, prostrating in the night and declaring His purity at length; Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that **this preoccupation will serve as a remedy for the non-believers' persecution**. Towards the conclusion, the sūrah shows the reason for the persistence of the obdurate: they are intoxicated with the fleeting pleasures of this world and have neglected the Hereafter — "whereas if they had pondered in their own being or existence, they would have recognised and understood their Creator and Maker."

That is the doorway into ayah 29. What is being offered is not obscure knowledge. It is a reminder.

## Ayah 29: "Verily, this is an admonition"

**إِنَّ هَٰذِهِ تَذْكِرَةٌ** — "Verily, this is an admonition." Ibn Kathir's gloss is short and precise: *this Sūrah is a reminder.* The word "this" points back at what the listener has just heard — the sūrah itself, its Paradise and its warning, is the *tadhkirah*, the reminder placed in his hands.

**فَمَنْ شَاءَ اتَّخَذَ إِلَىٰ رَبِّهِ سَبِيلًا** — "so whosoever wills, let him take a path to his Lord." Ibn Kathir explains *sabīl* as "a path and a way," and gives the sense of the whole phrase as: *whoever wishes to be guided by the Qur'an.* The door is not narrow and the condition is not elaborate. Wanting to be guided by this Book — that is the path.

And then Ibn Kathir places beside it a verse that carries the ayah's quiet grief: "And what loss have they if they had believed in Allah and in the Last Day?" (4:39). What would it have cost them? Nothing at all.

## Ayah 30: "But you cannot will, unless Allah wills"

**وَمَا تَشَاءُونَ إِلَّا أَنْ يَشَاءَ اللَّهُ** — "But you cannot will, unless Allah wills." Ibn Kathir: this means *no one is able to guide himself, enter into faith or bring about any benefit for himself, unless Allah wills.*

Read that carefully, because it is more searching than it first appears. It is not only guidance in the abstract that is placed beyond our reach; it is entering into faith, and it is bringing about *any benefit for oneself* at all. The one who has taken the path of ayah 29 is being told, in the very next breath, Who put him on it.

This is why Ibn Kathir's heading pairs the two halves — the Qur'an is a reminder, **and guidance comes from the help of Allah**. Ayah 29 tells you what to do. Ayah 30 tells you Whom to ask for it.

### "Ever All-Knowing, All-Wise"

**إِنَّ اللَّهَ كَانَ عَلِيمًا حَكِيمًا** — "Verily, Allah is Ever All-Knowing, All-Wise." Of all the names that could have closed the ayah, these are the two chosen: knowledge and wisdom.

Ibn Kathir explains what they answer: *He is Most Knowledgeable of who deserves to be guided. So, He makes guidance easy for him and He predestines for him that which will be a cause for it. However, whoever deserves misguidance, He averts guidance from him. Unto Him belongs the most excellent wisdom and the most irrefutable argument.*

Sit with the middle clause: **He predestines for him that which will be a cause for it.** Guidance is not only granted; the causes that lead to it are themselves arranged by Allah. And so, when a person finds himself wanting to be guided by this Book — the wanting that ayah 29 asks for — that wanting is not a credential he manufactured. It is already something being given to him.

## Ayah 31: admitted into His mercy

**يُدْخِلُ مَنْ يَشَاءُ فِي رَحْمَتِهِ ۚ وَالظَّالِمِينَ أَعَدَّ لَهُمْ عَذَابًا أَلِيمًا** — "He will admit to His mercy whom He wills, and as for the wrongdoers — He has prepared a painful torment."

Notice how the two halves are named. The first names no reason beyond His will: *whom He wills*. The second does not name a will at all; it names the people by a description — **the wrongdoers**, *al-ẓālimīn*.

Ibn Kathir's summary of the ayah is where the whole passage comes to rest: *He guides whomever He wishes and He leads astray whomever He wishes. Whoever He guides, there is no one who can lead him astray; and whoever He leads astray, there is no one who can guide him.*

There is enormous security in the first half of that sentence for anyone who has been given even the beginning of guidance. Whatever stands against him — persecution, as the sūrah has already described, or anything else — there is no one who can undo what Allah has done for him.

And note the word the ayah uses for the destination: not "Paradise," but **His mercy**. Earlier in the same sūrah, at ayah 22, the people of Paradise are addressed with "This is a reward for you, and your effort has been appreciated." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān comments that these expressions are made to them by way of congratulation, and that for the people of love, the Divine congratulatory expressions will outweigh all the other blessings of Paradise put together — because they are proof positive of Divine pleasure. Read alongside that, "His mercy" in ayah 31 names something warmer than an address.

## Living it

**Do not use ayah 30 as an excuse.** The order of the two ayat is worth attention: the invitation to take the path comes first, and the reminder about Allah's will comes second — it does not cancel the invitation that stands immediately before it. Ibn Kathir's words are that *no one is able to guide himself*.

**Turn the ayah into a request.** If no one can enter into faith or bring about any benefit for himself unless Allah wills it, then the most sensible response is to ask Him — to make *duʿāʾ*, calling on Allah, for guidance, for steadfastness, for a heart that wants what it should want. The same truth that undercuts self-congratulation is the truth that makes asking Him the most reasonable thing a person can do.

**Take ayah 29 at its word.** Ibn Kathir's reading of "let him take a path to his Lord" is simply: *whoever wishes to be guided by the Qur'an.* That is available today — one deliberate turn toward this Book, with the wish to be guided by it. And ask Him for the wishing first.

*"This is the end of the Tafsir of Surat Al-Insan. And all praise and thanks are due to Allah."*
